newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish flood swell hits Wroclaw, advances north.
newsitem.headline: Polish flood swell hits Wroclaw, advances north.

text.p: After week-long floods ravaged much of Poland, killing at least 30 people, citizens of Wroclaw who built sandbag barriers through the night appeared optimistic on Sunday that they had saved historic parts of their city.

"The (Old Town) square and the materially most precious part of Wroclaw were defended, thanks to the great solidarity and enormous efforts of the people," a provincial government spokesman, Ludwik Ryng, told Reuters by telephone from Wroclaw.
Wroclaw was hit overnight by the high-point in a surge of water storming north along the Odra River from the deluged south of Poland after days of rain, now mostly abated.

Ryng said an island with famous buildings and a university library with priceless books, including a vast German collection, had largely been rescued from damage, although a librarian said water was seeping into basement storerooms.
Officials said the main surge had passed the city of 650,000 people, which until 1945 was the German city Breslau, but suburbs and much of the centre were submerged.
Work continued to fight still-spreading water as helicopters clattered overhead rescuing those stranded on high-rise blocks in Wroclaw,

The deluge, the region's worst natural disaster in several centuries, also devastated swathes of the neighbouring Czech Republic during the week, where the central flood commission put the confirmed death toll to date at 28.

Floods forced hundreds more Czech villagers from their homes on Sunday as rescue workers pondered how to deal with the mess left behind as the tide passed. The surging waters also reached villages on the Slovak border in the south-east.
Hundreds of people living close to the river Morava in the village of Hodonin were moved to higher ground.
"Hodonin is threatened by a rolling mass of water," Pavel Urbancik of the local flood commission, told CTK news agency.
In Poland, the Odra swell advanced mercilessly on towns further north towards the German border, including Glogow and Brzeg Dolny, while 8,000 residents of the Legnica area were evacuated.
Deputy Environment Minister Krzysztof Szamalek told reporters that by the time it flowed along the border it might still cause some floods, but added: "It won't be a cataclysm."
A less dangerous swell of high water was also advancing along the Wisla River and was due to reach Warsaw early on Monday -- but Szamalek said it would not flood the capital.
Szamalek said that 2,400 sq kms were under water, down from 3,600 at the peak of the floods.
But even as waters receded further south, they left dozens of towns and hundreds of villages strewn with sewage, rubbish and dead farm animals, and bereft of clean water and power.
Health officials broadcast warnings to hundreds of thousands of returning evacuees and survivors to clean everything, sterilise water and beware of contaminated food.
Poles elsewhere brought gifts of soap, clothes, bread and blankets to collection points for transport south, but there were also reports on Polish radio of looting and profiteering.

The cabinet called an emergency meeting for Sunday evening and Parliament's speaker summoned its leading members to decide on calling an extraordinary sitting during the current recess to discuss finding money for relief and reconstruction.
Interior Minister Leszek Miller said on Saturday this would cost more than $1 billion, far exceeding the roughly $200 million already earmarked for the purpose.

Agriculture Minister Jaroslaw Kalinowski told public television his Peasant Party, the ex-communists' smaller partner in the ruling coalition, would propose on Tuesday that parliament amend this year's budget.

"We can see that the damage is enormous. We have had an enormous cataclysm," said Kalinowski, referring to overall losses rather than to crops. His ministry has said it will take weeks to estimate crop losses but has ruled out food shortages.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz were expected in Bonn on Monday for regular German-Polish consultations.
Germany has rallied to help, supplying money, equipment and expertise, while foreign aid also came from other sources.
